dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: NALP documents demographic representation, advancement disparities and recruitment-pipeline trends in U.S. law firms, but does not address legal AI capabilities, selective deployment, verification or AI-driven operating-model redesign. Its evidence therefore cannot establish a position on the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualification that positive aggregate pipeline outcomes can conceal unequal demographic trends. It documents a record overall share of summer associates of color alongside a sustained decline in Black representation, though it does not address the causes or overall scale of entry-level hiring contraction.

kp.k: Directory data establish the report's scope and limitations
kp.d: The report analyses legal workforce demographics, rather than AI or its effects. The 2024 directory includes race/ethnicity and gender information for 107,227 lawyers in 719 offices and 7,956 summer associates in 445 offices. Lawyer demographic data were reported as of February 1, 2024. Offices reporting an item as unknown or not collected are excluded from that demographic's aggregate figures, so coverage varies across measures.
qs: Law offices reported aggregate demographic data for their lawyers as of February 1, 2024.
Law offices that utilized the “not collected” or “unknown” reporting options for any demographic items are not included in the aggregate figures for that particular demographic(s).
The number of offices reporting one or more summer associates, including demographic information, was 445.

kp.k: Women and lawyers of color reach representation records
kp.d: In 2024, women accounted for 40.87% of lawyers, up approximately 1.4 percentage points and exceeding 40% for the first time. Lawyers of color accounted for 21.46%, while women of color accounted for 11.77%. Among associates, women reached 51.62%, people of color 31.46%, and women of color 18.76%; the latter group's growth accounted for most of the increase in associates of color.
qs: After comprising the majority of associates for the first time in 2023, women continued to make gains,
This increase can be largely attributed to growth in the percentage of women associates of color, which rose
by 1.2 points to 18.76%.

kp.k: Partnership diversity improves but remains substantially behind associates
kp.d: Women reached 28.83% of partners in 2024, compared with 27.76% in 2023; partners of color reached 12.73%, compared with 12.01%. Women of color reached 5.28%, exceeding 5% for the first time. Nikia L. Gray argues that attorneys of color face barriers to partnership and estimates that, at the current growth rate, partners of color would take nearly 27 years to reach today's associate representation. That estimate is a conditional extrapolation, not an observed promotion outcome.
qs: Women of color comprised more than 5% of all partners for the first time in 2024.
continue to examine the barriers that prevent attorneys of color from becoming partners if we hope to reduce that time.

kp.k: Equity partnership remains less diverse than non-equity partnership
kp.d: Separate equity-status reporting covers 21,212 partners at 170 offices/firms with tiered partnerships. Women represented 24.8% of equity partners versus 34.3% of non-equity partners; people of color represented 10.2% versus 15.2%. Within their respective partner cohorts, 59.5% of men, 48.3% of women and 46.5% of people of color were equity partners. Equity partners' overall share declined from 61.3% in 2011 to 56.3% in 2024. Some firms did not update their 2023 figures, and these results concern a separate reporting subset.
qs: Figures for 2024 are based on 170 offices/firms that have a tiered partnership and also reported information on equity and non-equity partner counts.
In some cases, firms did not update their figures from 2023.
Since partners of color are also counted in the men and women categories, percentages across these three categories do not add up to 100%.

kp.k: Partnership classifications reflect compensation and tax treatment
kp.d: Unless otherwise indicated, partner totals combine equity and non-equity partners. NALP defines equity partners through Schedule K-1 filing and receipt of no more than half their compensation on a fixed-income basis; non-equity partners receive more than half on a fixed basis and may or may not be eligible for equity partnership.
qs: The partner numbers in this report include both equity and non-equity partners, unless otherwise noted in Tables 6-8.
Equity Partners are those who file a Schedule K-1 tax form and receive no more than half their compensation on a fixed-income basis.
Non-equity Partners are those who receive more than half their compensation on a fixed basis.
These attorneys may or may not be generally eligible for equity partnership.

kp.k: Racial disaggregation reveals uneven associate representation
kp.d: Table 3 reports 2024 associate representation of 13.29% Asian, 7.40% Latinx, 6.40% Black or African American, 4.12% multiracial, 0.15% Native American or Alaska Native, and 0.10% Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander. Native American or Alaska Native representation declined from 0.24% in 2006; multiracial representation more than doubled from 1.79% in 2011. The report's aggregate gains therefore do not describe every racial or ethnic group's experience.
qs: While associates of color made gains overall, representation was flat for Native Hawaiian and other Pacific
Islander associates, and fell slightly for Native American and Alaska Native associates.

kp.k: Counsel and staff attorney demographics differ
kp.d: Women constituted 38.79% of counsel and 55.65% of non-traditional track/staff attorneys in 2024; people of color constituted 13.67% and 23.83%, respectively. Women had their highest representation in the staff attorney category, whose female share has fluctuated between 54% and 58% since NALP began tracking it in 2012. These are lawyer categories, not non-lawyer support roles.
qs: points to 55.65%. This lawyer category had the highest overall representation of women.
Staff attorneys of color increased by 0.2 percentage point to 23.83%.

kp.k: Summer associate gains mask Black representation declines
kp.d: Summer associates of color reached a record 43.07% in 2024, only slightly above 43.03% in 2022. Asian representation rose from 16.14% in 2023 to 17.94%, and multiracial representation from 4.64% to 5.14%. Black representation fell for a second consecutive year, from 11.85% in 2022 to 11.69% in 2023 and 10.24% in 2024. Women summer associates declined from 56.17% to 55.44%, while women of color declined from 26.40% to 26.08%. NALP treats summer classes as a potential indicator of subsequent associate demographics.

kp.k: Political explanation remains a concern, not established causation
kp.d: Gray connects concern about the Black summer associate decline to contemporaneous backlash against diversity initiatives and to NALP's separate finding that Black graduates' employment rate declined for the Class of 2023 despite record employment for the class overall. She explicitly cautions that these coincidences do not demonstrate causation and that short-term movements may be anomalies. Her warning that continued declines could affect Black associate representation is conditional.
qs: Coincidence does not indicate causation, and it is far too soon to conclude that the parties agitating for regressive change have succeeded, yet it bears paying close attention to.
If the decline continues, it could soon affect the representation of Black associates and possibly even the profession as a whole.
These signs may yet turn out to be limited anomalies that correct themselves in due course, but we cannot be complacent while we wait and see.

kp.k: Representation varies across firm sizes and locations
kp.d: Table 9 shows that firms with more than 1,000 lawyers reported women as 30.54% of partners, people of color as 15.31%, and women of color as 6.73%, compared with 28.83%, 12.73% and 5.28% overall. San Francisco reported 36.66% women partners. Associates of color represented 54.30% in Silicon Valley and 52.35% in Miami. Geographic tables require minimum reporting coverage and sometimes allocate firmwide figures to a reporting city under a stated concentration rule.
qs: Cities and states are included in the table if there are at least five reporting firms and 100 total partners or associates.
For multi-office firms that reported only firmwide figures, the information was attributed to the reporting city if at least 60% of the firm’s lawyers are in that city.

kp.k: Disability figures increase but reporting remains limited
kp.d: Among reporting offices/firms, lawyers with disabilities represented 2.54% of lawyers in 2024, compared with 1.99% in 2023; the 2024 figures were 3.20% for associates and 1.78% for partners. Table 15 covers 83,718 lawyers at 552 offices/firms and 5,471 summer associates at 298 offices/firms. NALP cautions that disability data are less widely reported and likely underreported; its separate graduate research found 7.3% of the Class of 2023 self-identified as having a disability.
qs: Overall, counts of individuals with disabilities, including zero, cover 83,718 lawyers and 5,471 summer associates.
Since reporting is still somewhat limited, trend information on lawyers with disabilities are not presented.

kp.k: LGBTQ representation rises most strongly in junior cohorts
kp.d: Reported LGBTQ representation reached 5.13% of lawyers in 2024, including 7.75% of associates and 2.75% of partners. Summer associate representation reached 12.92%, up from 5.73% in 2018. Table 16 covers 105,130 lawyers and 7,517 summer associates. These figures concern reporting populations rather than the entire legal profession.

kp.k: Non-binary counts rise, but detailed analysis remains constrained
kp.d: In the fifth year of collecting non-binary gender information, NALP reported 108 non-binary lawyers, compared with 79 in 2023, 42 in 2022, 20 in 2021 and nine in 2020. The 2024 count comprised 95 associates, eight partners, two staff attorneys and three counsel, with 32 non-binary summer associates reported separately. Reporting coverage was 78.3% of offices/firms for lawyers and 50.7% for summer associates, limiting more detailed analysis.
qs: Limited reporting of gender non-binary lawyers and summer associates also precludes more detailed analysis; however, counts are included in the text of the report.

kp.k: Veteran representation is lowest among associates
kp.d: Military veterans constituted 1.95% of lawyers in reporting offices/firms: 2.00% of partners, 1.62% of associates, and 2.82% of counsel and staff attorneys combined. Summer associate representation was 1.75%. Table 18 covers 98,800 lawyers and 6,794 summer associates; NALP does not present a veteran trend series because reporting remains limited.
qs: The percentage of lawyers who are military veterans was 1.95%. Representation of military veterans was
lowest amongst associates (1.62%).
Overall, military veteran counts, including zero, cover 98,800 lawyers and 6,794 summer associates.
